headline: Tiverton secures $1M grant for water line after PFAS well contamination
dek: The USDA award will help the North Tiverton Fire District begin extending public water to households whose private wells exceed Rhode Island's PFAS standard, while testing and the source investigation continue.
body: Tiverton has secured $1 million in federal assistance to begin extending public water service to homes whose private wells have been contaminated with per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, or PFAS. The money is being provided through the U.S. Department of Agriculture's Emergency Community Water Assistance program to the North Tiverton Fire District, according to a Sept. 29 announcement from the offices of U.S. Sens. Jack Reed and Sheldon Whitehouse and Rep. Gabe Amo.

The grant is aimed at the Crandall Road, Bulgarmarsh Road and Stafford Road areas, where Rhode Island officials are continuing to test private wells. The lawmakers' announcement said more than 100 wells tested so far had exceeded Rhode Island's 20-parts-per-trillion standard, with some results above 4,000 parts per trillion. The lawmakers had backed the district's application in a Sept. 8 letter to Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins, asking for emergency funding to restore reliable drinking water to affected homeowners.

The award does not resolve the wider water problem. [What's Up Newp](https://whatsupnewp.com/2026/10/tiverton-gets-1-million-in-federal-funding-for-emergency-water-line-after-pfas-contamination/) reported Oct. 1 that the grant will start the public-water extension, while testing and planning continue for other households. The publication said the town's effort is focused on homes with the most serious contamination first. A separate Providence Journal report, republished by [AOL](https://www.aol.com/articles/help-coming-tiverton-homeowners-contaminated-185020000.html), said town officials were seeking to put the first section in the ground before winter and had sent the project out to bid, but the full buildout will require additional money and coordination.

Tiverton's [municipal PFAS information page](https://www.tiverton.ri.gov/363/PFAS-Information) identifies the Crandall Road area as the subject of continuing investigation and posts updates from Sept. 15, Sept. 22 and Sept. 28. The town cautions that its concentration map shows the known or suspected area of impact, not a property-by-property finding. It tells residents to rely on Rhode Island Department of Environmental Management laboratory results and state guidance rather than assuming a home is safe or contaminated based only on its location.

RIDEM says on its [emerging-contaminants program page](https://dem.ri.gov/ecsdc-grants) that it detected PFAS above the state maximum contaminant level in a private well near Crandall Road and offered free testing to homes within a quarter-mile of the fire station or the initial detection. The agency says it is providing filtration systems at no cost to homeowners whose results exceed 20 parts per trillion. In its statewide emerging-contaminants program, DEM says it is testing more than 800 private wells in 26 communities and using activated-carbon or reverse-osmosis systems where eligible results are above the state standard.

The suspected source in Tiverton has not been established. Local reporting has noted the investigation's proximity to Tiverton Fire Station 3 and the historical use of PFAS-containing firefighting foam, but the state has not confirmed that the station caused the contamination. That distinction matters as officials decide whether public water, household treatment or other remedies are appropriate for each property.

For residents, the immediate change is a path toward a permanent water connection for at least the first phase of the response, rather than continued reliance on bottled water or individual treatment while results arrive. The lawmakers said construction is expected to be completed before the end of December, though the schedule remains dependent on design, bidding, permits and the district's work. Tiverton says it will continue posting test results, water-delivery information and public updates as the investigation develops.
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoDescription: A USDA grant will help Tiverton begin extending public water to homes with PFAS-contaminated private wells as testing continues.
sourceName: U.S. Senate Office of Jack Reed
